archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (variance-heavy defense)
archetype.definition: A team whose down-to-down defense and passing game still look like a fringe-playoff unit, but whose 0-4 start came from close losses, special-teams bleed and explosive pass plays allowed, more than from being outplayed snap after snap.

report.headline: Close losses, leaky deep coverage and a dead run game, not a lost season.
report.take:
Houston is 0-4, and the first thing to say is that the record overstates how bad this has been. Three of the four losses came by five points or fewer (36-31, 19-17, 34-30), and the Texans rank last in wins over expected at -2.18, the unluckiest mark in the league. That isn't a clean bill of health. Net EPA is 25th and point differential is 26th, so this is a below-average team so far. It is a below-average team that should have a win or two, and one coming off a 12-5 season with the league's second-best defense by EPA.

The defense is the strangest part of the profile. On a play-by-play basis it still wins: opponents' success rate is 4th-lowest in the league, the sack rate is 2nd, and the run defense is a respectable 12th. But when it loses a snap, it loses big. Houston ranks 29th in explosive pass rate allowed and 29th in EPA on deep throws. That is a boom-or-bust shape, not a broken unit, and two of the four opponents were the league's 2nd- and 3rd-ranked offenses (Dallas and Buffalo), who scored 34 and 36. Against Cincinnati and Indianapolis the defense allowed 20 and 19. Explosive-play rates are among the noisier defensive numbers, and this group's success rate argues the deep leaks will tighten. Losing Azeez Al-Shaair, a 92%-snap linebacker, and possibly Kenneth Murray (concussion evaluation) cuts against that in the short term.

On offense, C.J. Stroud is carrying it. The passing game is a league-average 15th in EPA, at 285 yards a game. The run game is the worst in football by any measure: 2.96 yards per carry (32nd), a 29.4% success rate (32nd) and a 25.9% stuff rate (28th). Backs average 2.32 yards before contact, which is middling. That leaves barely half a yard after contact, so the problem isn't only the line. Week 1's 124 rushing yards look like the outlier; the last three games produced 60, 70 and 62. Add special teams at -3.61 EPA per game (27th), which comes to roughly 14 points of field-position and kicking value over four weeks, more than the 11 combined points Houston lost its three close games by. The penalties hurt too: 7.8 per game, with the offensive line drawing 4.3 of them (25th).

The path back runs through a soft schedule. Seven of the remaining 13 opponents rank 23rd or worse in offensive EPA, which is exactly the kind of slate that punishes a defense less for giving up the occasional explosive play. Nico Collins has played only two games but drew nine targets a game when on the field, and Tank Dell's practice window is opening. A healthier receiver room plus regression in close games and on special teams should get this team back toward .500 football. Whether that's enough to dig out of 0-4 with Jacksonville at 3-1 is a different question.

strengths.title: Defense still wins most snaps
strengths.body: Opponents succeed on only 40.2% of plays (4th-best allowed rate) and Houston's sack rate is 2nd in the league. The pass rush and early-down discipline from last year's elite unit are intact; the damage is concentrated in a few explosive completions. Success rate tends to be the more stable signal, so this is the part to trust.

strengths.title: Stroud keeps the passing game afloat
strengths.body: Despite zero help from the run game, the pass offense sits 15th in EPA. Stroud is averaging about 285 yards a game. The Dallas game (+15.2 pass EPA) showed the ceiling when protection holds. With Collins back in the lineup and Dell possibly returning, the target tree improves on paper. Right now the volume is spread across a tight end (Schultz) and depth receivers.

strengths.title: The record is the unluckiest in football
strengths.body: Winning zero of three one-score games and sitting last in wins over expected is the kind of result that tends to even out. Houston was +1.89 and +2.46 over expected in 2023 and 2025 with this coach, so it isn't a structural late-game problem.

concerns.title: Deep balls are killing the defense
concerns.body: Houston is 29th in both explosive pass rate allowed and deep-throw EPA, and that is the main reason a top-five success-rate defense is allowing 27.3 points a game. Some of it is the opposition, with two top-three offenses on the schedule. Losing Al-Shaair to a groin injury and possibly Murray thins the second level. That makes coverage busts harder to clean up, so this may not tighten immediately.

concerns.title: A run game with nothing behind it
concerns.body: Last in yards per carry and run success, with a stuff rate of 28th. Yards before contact are only middling (17th), so the backs are also adding almost nothing after contact. This is likely to persist and leaves Stroud facing long-yardage downs. The 7.2% sack rate allowed and 3.0-second average time to throw compound it.

concerns.title: Special teams and penalties leak points
concerns.body: At -3.61 EPA per game, the third phase has cost more than the combined margin of the three close losses. The offensive line's 4.3 penalties a game (25th) keep stalling drives. Week 3 at Indianapolis, with just 14 penalty yards, was the cleanest game of the year, so discipline is fixable. Special teams has no visible fix in the data.

trend.note: Scoring has gone 31, 6, 17, 30 and pass EPA has swung from -9.7 against Cincinnati to +15.2 against Dallas. The offense is boom-or-bust week to week, and it hasn't yet produced a game where the defense and offense both played well.

nextGame.headline: A favorable matchup for Stroud, but seven road points is steep.
nextGame.body:
Tennessee is the weakest offense Houston has faced: 13.8 points a game (31st) and last in yardage. The Titans are also the most run-heavy team in the league, with a pass rate over expected of -10.5. That plays away from Houston's real weakness, deep coverage, and toward its strengths. The Titans' own defense has the same problem Houston's does, only worse. It is 26th against the pass, 31st in deep-throw EPA, and its pressure rate ranks 23rd. Stroud should have time to push the ball downfield. The Titans also own the league's worst special teams, which may neutralize Houston's biggest hidden leak for a week.

Availability cuts both ways. Houston is without Al-Shaair and may be without Murray, the two linebackers most exposed to a Tennessee offense that lives on the run. The Titans' stuff rate allowed is 5th-best, so the run game they're bringing is real. Tennessee, though, just put two guards on injured reserve, including Fernando Carmona (67% of snaps), which should help Houston's front, already 3rd in sacks. Collins's availability is worth checking; he has appeared in only two of four games.

keyMatchups.title: Stroud deep versus Titans secondary
keyMatchups.body: Tennessee allows the second-worst deep-throw EPA in the league and doesn't generate much pressure. Houston should lean on the pass more than its slightly run-leaning tendencies suggest. The run game won't move the ball against a middling Titans run defense.

keyMatchups.title: Titans run game versus thinned linebackers
keyMatchups.body: Tennessee runs more than anyone relative to expectation and rarely gets stuffed. With Al-Shaair out and Murray questionable, this is where the Titans can stay on schedule and shorten the game. Their two injured guards are the counterweight.

keyMatchups.title: Houston pass rush versus patchwork guards
keyMatchups.body: Houston's sack rate is 2nd in the league. Tennessee has protected well so far (6 sacks allowed), but that was with guards now on injured reserve. If the interior holds up, the Titans can grind; if it doesn't, Cam Ward's limited passing game has no answer.

nextGame.watch: Whether Houston's defense stops the Titans on early downs without its top two linebackers. If Tennessee runs efficiently, this becomes a short, low-scoring game where a seven-point margin is hard to reach.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect improvement. The schedule eases considerably: the Chargers, Eagles, Packers, Titans, Steelers, Colts and Giants all rank 23rd or worse in offensive EPA. That should take the edge off the explosive-pass problem and let the top-five success-rate defense look more like last year's. Close-game luck and special teams should also drift back toward neutral. That alone is worth a win or two. The run game is the part not to expect much from; it has been bottom-of-the-league across three straight games, with the problems spread between the blocking and the backs.

The ceiling is roughly a .500 finish or a bit above. From 0-4, with Jacksonville at 3-1 and two meetings left against the Jaguars plus Baltimore at home, the playoffs require something close to an 8-5 or 9-4 finish. That's possible against this slate but not the base case. A healthy Collins and a returning Dell are the biggest upside levers. The linebacker injuries are the biggest near-term risk.
swingFactors: Al-Shaair and Murray returning to the linebacker corps
Collins and Dell healthy alongside Stroud
Special teams moving from bleeding points to neutral

bets.reason: By net EPA the two teams are close (-0.094 vs -0.112) and their point differentials are nearly identical (-6.3 vs -7.0 per game). Laying a touchdown on the road against a division rival is a lot for a team that is 0-4 against the spread. Tennessee's run-heavy, clock-shortening style also works against margin.

Titans games average about 34.6 combined points (13.8 scored, 20.8 allowed), and Tennessee is last in pass rate over expected. Houston's non-elite opponents scored 20 and 19, and the Texans' own run game can't drain clock efficiently either way. The main risk is Stroud hitting deep shots against a Titans secondary that ranks 31st in deep EPA.

confidence.note: Four-game sample against a front-loaded schedule; the strong prior from 2025 and the extreme close-game luck both point upward, but linebacker injuries cloud the short term.
